cues.text: Isidore Presides
In December 633, bishops of the Visigothic kingdom of Spain gathered at Toledo under the presidency of St. Isidore of Seville .
By then, he was the most learned churchman in the Spanish kingdom, already deep into his Etymologiae ’s vast encyclopedic labor.
Isidore's own intellectual seriousness shaped the council's agenda decisively, giving it a scope and rigor unusual among regional councils of the early medieval West.
A Mandate for Seminaries
The council's most consequential canon required every bishop in the kingdom to establish a cathedral school for the systematic training of clergy.
It was an early and remarkably far-sighted mandate for what would, many centuries later, become the seminary system the wider Catholic Church only adopted universally after the Council of Trent.
The canon specified instruction in Scripture, canon law, and the liturgy, treating clerical formation as a matter of settled, structural policy rather than local custom.
Liturgical Standardization
Fourth Toledo also worked to standardize liturgical practice across the Spanish Church, addressing variations in the Mass and Divine Office across the kingdom's provinces.
It affirmed Scripture and the received councils as the basis for settling such disputes.

This work was consistent with Isidore's broader project, pursued across his long episcopate, of consolidating and organizing the intellectual and liturgical life of a Church still working out its identity after its Visigothic rulers' recent conversion from Arianism.
Royal Succession and Church Discipline
Beyond matters of clergy and liturgy, the council addressed royal succession and the treatment of the kingdom’s Jewish population under recent, often harsh royal decrees.

It urged moderation in enforcement while upholding the underlying policy—a mixture of pastoral concern and political entanglement between the Visigothic crown and Catholic hierarchy, characteristic of councils convened in this newly unified kingdom.
Legacy
Fourth Toledo's seminary decree anticipated, by the better part of a millennium, reforms the wider Latin Church would not adopt as universal policy until Trent.

Its broader work of liturgical and disciplinary consolidation helped make Visigothic Spain, for a time, one of the more intellectually serious and well-organized regional churches of the early medieval West.
Isidore himself died only three years later.
The council he presided over remained a reference point for subsequent Toledan councils.
Across the following decades, they refined the structures of a Church his own vast learning had done so much to shape.
